title: Acute Migraine Headache Consultation
transcript:
Doctor: Good morning, Mr. Robert. How can I help you today?
Patient: Good morning Doctor. I have been having severe throbbing headaches for the past 3 days, mostly on the left side of my head. Um, it gets worse with bright light and loud sounds.
Doctor: I see. Are you experiencing any nausea, vomiting, or visual disturbances?
Patient: Yes, Doctor. I feel nauseous, like I want to throw up whenever the headache peaks. No vision changes though.
Doctor: Have you taken any medication for this?
Patient: I tried taking OTC ibuprofen 400 mg twice a day, but it barely helped.
Doctor: Okay. Your vitals show blood pressure is 120/80 mmHg and temperature is normal at 98.6 degrees F. Physical examination is unremarkable. I am diagnosing acute migraine headache. I am prescribing Sumatriptan 50 mg to take at the onset of severe pain, along with Paracetamol 500 mg for relief. Please rest in a dark quiet room and drink plenty of fluids.
Patient: Thank you Doctor. When should I follow up?
Doctor: Follow up in 1 week if the migraine episodes continue.
reference_summary: Patient Robert presented with a 3-day history of severe left-sided throbbing headache accompanied by photophobia and nausea. Prior treatment with OTC ibuprofen 400 mg provided minimal relief. Vitals were normal (BP 120/80 mmHg, Temp 98.6 F). Diagnosed with acute migraine headache. Prescribed Sumatriptan 50 mg and Paracetamol 500 mg with instructions to rest in dark room and follow up in 1 week.

title: Upper Respiratory Tract Infection
transcript:
Doctor: Hello Ms. Sarah. What brings you in today?
Patient: Hi Doctor. I've had a dry cough, sore throat, and low fever for about 5 days. Uh, I also feel very tired.
Doctor: Let me check your throat and lungs. Your throat looks inflamed, but your lungs are clear on auscultation. Temperature is 100.4 F.
Patient: Is it pneumonia Doctor?
Doctor: No, your chest is clear. This is a viral upper respiratory infection. Have you taken anything?
Patient: Just warm water and throat lozenges.
Doctor: Excellent. I advise rest, increased hydration, and Paracetamol 500 mg every 8 hours as needed for fever and throat pain. No antibiotics are necessary for viral infections.
Patient: Understood. How long will this last?
Doctor: Symptoms should resolve in 7 to 10 days. Follow up if fever exceeds 102 F or if shortness of breath develops.
reference_summary: Patient Sarah presented with a 5-day history of dry cough, sore throat, fatigue, and low-grade fever (100.4 F). Examination revealed inflamed pharynx with clear lung fields. Diagnosed with viral upper respiratory tract infection. Managed conservatively with rest, hydration, and Paracetamol 500 mg. Advised to return if fever exceeds 102 F or dyspnea develops.

title: Hypertension Routine Review
transcript:
Doctor: Hello Mr. David, good to see you. How have you been feeling on the Amlodipine 5 mg?
Patient: Hello Doctor. I feel fine overall, no chest pain or shortness of breath. But I noticed slight ankle swelling in the evenings for the last 2 weeks.
Doctor: Let us check your vitals. Your blood pressure is 138/86 mmHg and heart rate is 72 bpm. Ankle swelling is a common mild side effect of Amlodipine. Have you been taking your medication regularly?
Patient: Yes Doctor, every morning without fail.
Doctor: Good. Your blood pressure control is satisfactory. We will maintain your Amlodipine 5 mg daily and order a routine renal function and electrolyte blood test. Please elevate your legs when sitting to reduce swelling.
Patient: Sure Doctor. Should I return next month?
Doctor: Yes, return in 4 weeks with your lab results.
reference_summary: Patient David attended routine hypertension follow-up on Amlodipine 5 mg daily. Reported mild evening pedal edema for 2 weeks with no chest pain or dyspnea. BP was 138/86 mmHg, HR 72 bpm. Medication adherence is excellent. Advised leg elevation, ordered renal function tests, and scheduled follow-up in 4 weeks.

title: Acute Gastroenteritis Consultation
transcript:
Doctor: Good afternoon Mrs. Linda. What brings you to the clinic?
Patient: Doctor, I have had terrible watery diarrhea and vomiting since yesterday evening, probably 6 episodes of diarrhea. My stomach has painful cramps.
Doctor: Any fever, blood in stool, or recent travel or takeout food?
Patient: No blood, but I did eat seafood at a restaurant two nights ago. I feel very thirsty and dizzy when standing up.
Doctor: Examination shows mild abdominal tenderness without guarding. Vitals show BP 106/68 mmHg, heart rate 94 bpm, temperature 99.2 F. You have acute gastroenteritis with mild dehydration.
Patient: Do I need an antibiotic Doctor?
Doctor: No, most gastroenteritis is self-limiting. I prescribe Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS) solution, Ondansetron 4 mg for vomiting, and Loperamide if diarrhea persists. Stick to a bland diet.
Patient: When should I seek emergency care?
Doctor: Return immediately if you cannot keep fluids down, experience high fever, or notice blood in your stool.
reference_summary: Patient Linda presented with acute gastroenteritis and mild dehydration following recent seafood consumption. Symptoms include frequent watery diarrhea, vomiting, and abdominal cramping for 24 hours. Physical examination revealed mild diffuse abdominal tenderness. Vitals showed mild tachycardia (HR 94) and borderline hypotension. Prescribed oral rehydration salts, Ondansetron 4 mg, and dietary guidance.

title: Type 2 Diabetes Routine Review
transcript:
Doctor: Good morning Mr. Michael. Let us review your glycemic control.
Patient: Good morning Doctor. I have been taking Metformin 500 mg twice daily. However, I have noticed increased thirst and frequent urination at night for 3 weeks.
Doctor: Your fasting blood glucose today is 182 mg/dL and your HbA1c is 8.6%, which is above our target of 7.0%. Have you had any blurred vision, numbness, or tingling in your feet?
Patient: Slight numbness in my toes, but no vision problems.
Doctor: Examination reveals intact peripheral pulses but slightly reduced vibration sensation in the distal toes. Blood pressure is 132/82 mmHg. We need to escalate therapy.
Patient: What changes will we make Doctor?
Doctor: I am increasing your Metformin to 1000 mg twice daily with meals and adding Empagliflozin 10 mg once daily. We will also consult our dietitian for medical nutrition therapy.
Patient: When will we recheck my blood levels?
Doctor: We will recheck your renal function in 2 weeks and your HbA1c in 3 months.
reference_summary: Patient Michael attended diabetic management review with suboptimal glycemic control (HbA1c 8.6%, fasting glucose 182 mg/dL) presenting with polyuria and polydipsia. Examination showed mild peripheral sensory neuropathy in distal toes. Intensified medication from Metformin 500 mg to Metformin 1000 mg twice daily plus Empagliflozin 10 mg daily with renal panel in 2 weeks and follow-up in 3 months.

title: Acute Otitis Media (Pediatric)
transcript:
Doctor: Hello Mrs. Clark, how is little Tommy doing?
Patient: Doctor, Tommy is 4 years old and has been tugging his right ear and crying all night. He has had a fever of 101.5 F and refuses to eat.
Doctor: Let me inspect his ears, nose, and throat. The left tympanic membrane is clear. However, the right tympanic membrane is markedly erythematous, bulging, with poor mobility.
Patient: Is it an ear infection Doctor?
Doctor: Yes, Tommy has acute otitis media of the right ear. His chest and lungs are clear.
Patient: Will he need an antibiotic?
Doctor: Yes, given the high fever and severe ear pain, I am prescribing Amoxicillin suspension 40 mg/kg/day divided twice daily for 7 days. Also use pediatric Paracetamol syrup 160 mg every 6 hours as needed for fever and pain.
Patient: When should he improve?
Doctor: Fever and pain should decrease within 48 to 72 hours. If he is not better by day 3, please bring him back.
reference_summary: Four-year-old Tommy presented with right ear pain, nocturnal crying, irritability, and fever of 101.5 F. Otoscopic examination revealed right acute otitis media with erythematous, bulging tympanic membrane. Diagnosed with acute suppurative otitis media. Prescribed oral Amoxicillin suspension for 7 days and pediatric Paracetamol with review in 72 hours if unimproved.

title: Mechanical Lower Back Pain
transcript:
Doctor: Hello Mr. James. What can I do for you today?
Patient: Hi Doctor. I injured my lower back 4 days ago while lifting heavy furniture at home. The pain is aching and stiff, rated 7 out of 10 across my lumbar spine.
Doctor: Does the pain shoot down into your legs, or do you have any numbness in your groin or loss of bowel or bladder control?
Patient: No shooting pain into the legs and no bladder or bowel issues at all. Just stiffness and localized muscle soreness.
Doctor: On examination, you have lumbar paraspinal muscle spasms and tenderness, but straight leg raise test is negative bilaterally and lower limb neurological examination is normal.
Patient: Is it a slipped disc Doctor?
Doctor: No, findings are consistent with acute mechanical lumbar muscle strain without radiculopathy. I advise avoiding heavy lifting, applying alternating ice and heat, and staying gently active.
Patient: What can I take for the pain?
Doctor: I am prescribing Naproxen 500 mg twice daily with food for 5 days and Cyclobenzaprine 5 mg at bedtime. Follow up if pain persists after 2 weeks.
reference_summary: Patient James presented with a 4-day history of acute lower back pain following heavy lifting. Red flag screening was negative for cauda equina and radiculopathy. Physical exam demonstrated lumbar paraspinal spasm with negative straight leg raise test and intact neurological exam. Diagnosed with acute mechanical lumbar strain. Prescribed Naproxen 500 mg, muscle relaxant, active mobilization, and follow-up in 2 weeks.

title: Generalized Anxiety Disorder Review
transcript:
Doctor: Good morning Ms. Rachel, how have you been coping lately?
Patient: Good morning Doctor. I have been feeling overwhelmed by constant worry and restlessness for the past 6 months. I cannot sleep more than 3 hours a night, my heart races, and my chest feels tight.
Doctor: Have you had panic attacks or feelings of impending doom? Any thoughts of self-harm?
Patient: No thoughts of harming myself. But I get trembling and tension headaches whenever I try to relax at home.
Doctor: Your vital signs show BP 124/78 mmHg, heart rate 86 bpm, and thyroid function tests done last week were normal. Your GAD-7 screening score is 16, indicating moderate to severe generalized anxiety disorder.
Patient: Can medication help me sleep and calm my mind?
Doctor: Yes. I recommend starting Escitalopram 10 mg once daily in the morning, alongside cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) with our clinical psychologist. For severe sleep disruption, take Melatonin 3 mg at bedtime.
Patient: When should I notice improvement?
Doctor: Escitalopram takes 2 to 4 weeks to show full therapeutic benefit. Let us schedule a follow-up in 3 weeks to monitor response and side effects.
reference_summary: Patient Rachel presented with a 6-month history of pervasive anxiety, insomnia, palpitations, muscle tension, and restlessness (GAD-7 score 16). Organic causes excluded with normal thyroid labs. Denied suicidal ideation. Diagnosed with Generalized Anxiety Disorder. Initiated on Escitalopram 10 mg daily, CBT referral, and sleep hygiene counseling with scheduled 3-week clinical review.

title: Acute Uncomplicated Cystitis (UTI)
transcript:
Doctor: Hello Ms. Emily, what symptoms are bothering you today?
Patient: Doctor, I have had a severe burning sensation when urinating for 2 days. I need to run to the bathroom every 20 minutes, and my urine looks cloudy.
Doctor: Any flank pain, high fever, chills, or nausea?
Patient: No back pain, no chills. Just pelvic discomfort and painful urination.
Doctor: Your temperature is 98.4 F and abdomen is soft with mild suprapubic tenderness. No costovertebral angle tenderness. Point-of-care urinalysis shows positive leukocytes, positive nitrites, and trace hematuria.
Patient: Is it a bladder infection Doctor?
Doctor: Yes, this is acute uncomplicated urinary tract infection (cystitis). You do not have signs of upper kidney infection (pyelonephritis).
Patient: What antibiotic will clear it?
Doctor: I am prescribing Nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for 5 days. Drink at least 2 liters of water daily and take Phenazopyridine 200 mg for 2 days to relieve the burning sensation.
Patient: When should the symptoms stop?
Doctor: Symptoms should markedly improve in 24 to 48 hours. Follow up if you develop flank pain or fever.
reference_summary: Patient Emily presented with a 2-day history of dysuria, urinary frequency, and suprapubic discomfort. Urinalysis was positive for nitrites and leukocyte esterase, consistent with acute uncomplicated cystitis. Systemic and pyelonephritis signs were absent. Managed with oral Nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for 5 days, urinary analgesic, and hydration instructions.

title: Asthma Mild Exacerbation
transcript:
Doctor: Hello Mr. Daniel. I hear you have been wheezing today.
Patient: Yes Doctor. My asthma has flared up over the last 3 days after catching a cold. I wake up coughing at night and feel shortness of breath and chest tightness when climbing stairs.
Doctor: How often have you been using your blue albuterol rescue inhaler?
Patient: Around 4 to 5 times a day, but the relief only lasts about an hour.
Doctor: Let us check your lungs and vitals. Oxygen saturation is 96% on room air, respiratory rate is 20 breaths/min. Auscultation reveals expiratory wheezing bilaterally. Peak expiratory flow rate is 340 L/min, which is 70% of your personal best.
Patient: Do I need a nebulizer Doctor?
Doctor: We will administer one in-clinic Albuterol nebulizer treatment now. For home management, we will step up your therapy to a combined Fluticasone/Salmeterol inhaler twice daily and a 5-day course of oral Prednisone 40 mg daily.
Patient: When should I come back for a checkup?
Doctor: Return to clinic in 5 days for a peak flow recheck, or go to the emergency department if you experience severe shortness of breath not relieved by inhalers.
reference_summary: Patient Daniel presented with mild-to-moderate asthma exacerbation secondary to viral upper respiratory tract infection. Reported nocturnal cough, dyspnea, and frequent Albuterol rescue use. Exam showed bilateral expiratory wheezing with peak flow at 70% of baseline and SaO2 96%. Stepped up to Fluticasone/Salmeterol maintenance plus 5-day oral Prednisone 40 mg burst and 5-day follow-up.
